title: Delivery: Helm, Kustomize and GitOps
subtitle: Charts, overlays, GitOps, progressive delivery and CI for Kubernetes
description: Ship to Kubernetes the way production teams do: write robust Helm charts, layer environments with Kustomize, reconcile from Git with Argo CD or Flux, roll out gradually with canaries, and gate everything in CI.
outcomes: Author and publish Helm charts with schema, hooks and tests
Structure Kustomize bases and overlays per environment
Run GitOps with Argo CD or Flux and handle drift and pruning
Release progressively and validate manifests in CI

lessons.title: Helm in depth: templates, hooks and dependencies
lessons.summary: Write real charts: named templates, values schema, hooks, tests, subchart dependencies and OCI registries.
objectives: Write templates with helpers, conditionals and required values
Use hooks and helm test, and publish charts to an OCI registry

sections.title: About this example: helpers and a deployment template
sections.body: This is a fragment of `templates/_helpers.tpl` followed by the use of those helpers in `templates/deployment.yaml`. It is not a standalone manifest, so it is shown as text. Look at `define`/`include` for reusable names and labels, `required` which fails the render if a value is missing, and `toYaml | nindent` which splices a values block with the right indentation.

sections.title: _helpers.tpl and deployment.yaml
sections.note: The `checksum/config` annotation changes whenever the ConfigMap changes, which forces a rollout - Helm does not restart pods on ConfigMap changes by itself.

sections.title: About this example: values and schema
sections.body: Two files are shown: `values.yaml` with safe defaults and `values.schema.json`, a JSON Schema that constrains them. The schema is checked by every Helm command that reads values, so a typo such as `replicaCount: "three"` fails before rendering. Look at `required`, `enum`, `minimum` and `additionalProperties: false`, which catches misspelled keys.

sections.title: About this example: hook, test and dependency commands
sections.body: This is a pre-upgrade migration Job (a complete manifest, so it gets a Run button) using Helm hook annotations. A hook resource is not part of the release: Helm creates it at the named moment, waits for completion, then deletes it according to the delete policy. Look at `helm.sh/hook`, `hook-weight` for ordering and `hook-delete-policy`, which is what keeps old Jobs from piling up.

sections.title: templates/migrate-job.yaml rendered
sections.code:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: shop-api-migrate
  annotations:
    helm.sh/hook: pre-install,pre-upgrade
    helm.sh/hook-weight: "0"
    helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded
spec:
  backoffLimit: 1
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: registry.example.com/shop/api:1.8.2
          command: ["./migrate", "up"]

sections.title: About this example: the release workflow
sections.body: These commands run on a workstation with `helm` and cluster access. `helm dependency update` resolves `Chart.yaml` dependencies into `charts/` and writes `Chart.lock`; `helm lint --strict` and `helm test` verify the chart; `helm push` publishes it to an OCI registry. Read the `STATUS` and `REVISION` columns in the upgrade output, and note that OCI charts are referenced as `oci://` with no `helm repo add`.

sections.title: Dependencies, lint, upgrade, test and OCI push
sections.code:
helm dependency update shop-api
helm lint shop-api --strict -f values-prod.yaml
helm upgrade --install shop shop-api -n shop --create-namespace -f values-prod.yaml --atomic --timeout 5m
helm test shop -n shop
helm package shop-api
helm push shop-api-0.4.0.tgz oci://registry.example.com/charts

lessons.title: Kustomize: bases, overlays and patches
lessons.summary: Customize plain manifests without templates: bases, overlays, strategic merge and JSON patches, generators and per-environment config.
objectives: Structure a base and per-environment overlays
Use configMapGenerator and images to drive environment config

sections.title: Template-free customization
sections.body:
Kustomize works on valid YAML. A **base** holds complete manifests; an **overlay** points at the base and layers changes on top - a different replica count, image tag, namespace or extra labels. Nothing is parameterized with placeholders, so the base can still be applied on its own. It is built into kubectl: `kubectl kustomize` renders and `kubectl apply -k` applies.

This fits teams that want to read exactly what will be deployed, and it pairs naturally with GitOps because the overlay directory is the environment.

sections.title: About this example: the base
sections.body: This is the base `deployment.yaml`, a complete valid manifest, so it can be applied directly with the Run button. The base `kustomization.yaml` that lists it appears in the next example. Look at the image tag `latest` placeholder and the single replica: both are meant to be overridden by overlays rather than edited here.

sections.title: base/deployment.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: shop-api
  labels:
    app: shop-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: shop-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: shop-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/shop/api:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: shop-api-config

sections.title: About this example: the production overlay
sections.body: This is `overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml` with its patch file, shown together as text since they are separate files. Look at `resources` pulling in the base, `images` rewriting the tag without a patch, `configMapGenerator` producing a hashed ConfigMap name, and the two kinds of patch: a strategic-merge file and an inline JSON 6902 operation that targets one object by kind and name.

sections.title: overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml and replicas-patch.yaml
sections.code:
# overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: shop-prod
namePrefix: prod-
resources:
  - ../../base
  - ingress.yaml
images:
  - name: registry.example.com/shop/api
    newTag: 1.8.2
commonLabels:
  env: prod
configMapGenerator:
  - name: shop-api-config
    behavior: create
    literals:
      - LOG_LEVEL=info
      - FEATURE_X=on
patches:
  - path: replicas-patch.yaml
  - target:
      kind: Deployment
      name: shop-api
    patch: |-
      - op: add
        path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources
        value:
          requests: {cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi}
          limits: {memory: 512Mi}

# overlays/prod/replicas-patch.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: shop-api
spec:
  replicas: 4

sections.title: About this example: render, diff and apply
sections.body: These commands render the prod overlay, preview the change against the live cluster, then apply it. `kubectl kustomize` is read-only; `kubectl diff -k` asks the API server to compute the difference; `apply -k` sends it. In the output look at the generated ConfigMap name with a content hash suffix, which makes a config change roll the Deployment automatically.

sections.title: Render, diff and apply an overlay
sections.code:
kubectl kustomize overlays/prod | grep -E '^(kind|  name|  replicas)|image:'
kubectl diff -k overlays/prod
kubectl apply -k overlays/prod

sections.title: Keep overlays small and avoid secrets in Git
sections.body: If an overlay needs more than a few patches, the base is probably missing a concept. `secretGenerator` only base64-encodes data; commit encrypted references (Sealed Secrets, SOPS or External Secrets) instead of raw values.

modules.title: Pipelines: GitOps, rollout and CI
modules.summary: Reconcile from Git, release gradually and gate with CI.

lessons.title: GitOps with Argo CD and Flux
lessons.summary: Make Git the source of truth: pull-based reconciliation, sync, drift detection and pruning with Argo CD and Flux.
objectives: Write an Argo CD Application and Flux GitRepository plus Kustomization
Control drift, self-heal and pruning safely

sections.title: Git as the source of truth
sections.body:
GitOps means the desired state lives in Git and an in-cluster controller continuously **pulls** it and reconciles the cluster. CI never needs cluster credentials: it commits an image tag, and the controller applies it. A rollback is a `git revert`, and an audit trail is the commit history.

Two tools dominate. **Argo CD** gives an Application model with a UI and diff view. **Flux** is a set of controllers (source, kustomize, helm, notification) driven entirely by CRDs. Both detect **drift** - live state differing from Git - and can correct it.

sections.title: About this example: an Argo CD Application
sections.body: This is a complete Argo CD `Application`, applied with `kubectl apply` in the `argocd` namespace (the Argo CD CRDs must be installed). It tells Argo CD which repo path to render and where to deploy it. Look at `source.path` and `targetRevision`, and at `syncPolicy`: `automated` with `prune` deletes resources removed from Git and `selfHeal` reverts manual edits.

sections.title: argocd Application
sections.code:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: shop-api-prod
  namespace: argocd
  finalizers:
    - resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io
spec:
  project: shop
  source:
    repoURL: https://git.example.com/platform/shop-deploy.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: overlays/prod
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: shop-prod
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
      - PruneLast=true
    retry:
      limit: 3
      backoff: {duration: 10s, factor: 2, maxDuration: 3m}

sections.title: About this example: Flux sources and Kustomization
sections.body: These two complete Flux objects work together: a `GitRepository` that fetches the repo every minute and a `Kustomization` that builds a path from it and applies it. Look at `interval` (poll and reconcile period), `prune: true`, `wait`/`timeout` for health gating, and `sourceRef` linking the two. Flux's Kustomization is not the same kind as Kustomize's kustomization.yaml, but it runs it.

sections.title: Flux GitRepository and Kustomization
sections.code:
apiVersion: source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: GitRepository
metadata:
  name: shop-deploy
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 1m
  url: https://git.example.com/platform/shop-deploy.git
  ref:
    branch: main
  secretRef:
    name: git-readonly-token
---
apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Kustomization
metadata:
  name: shop-prod
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 10m
  path: ./overlays/prod
  prune: true
  wait: true
  timeout: 5m
  targetNamespace: shop-prod
  sourceRef:
    kind: GitRepository
    name: shop-deploy

sections.title: About this example: observing sync state
sections.body: These commands show what each tool believes about the cluster. `argocd app get` prints sync status (does live match Git) and health (are workloads running); `flux get kustomizations` shows the last applied revision. Look at `OutOfSync`, which signals drift or an unsynced commit, and at the revision hash, which should match the commit you merged.

sections.title: Check sync status and force a reconcile

argocd app get shop-api-prod
argocd app diff shop-api-prod
flux get kustomizations
flux reconcile kustomization shop-prod --with-source

sections.title: Prune and self-heal are sharp tools
sections.body: Enable `prune` only after the repo path is correct: pointing an app at an empty directory deletes everything it owns. Protect stateful resources with `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: Prune=false`, keep Secrets out of plain Git, and separate the app repo from the deploy (config) repo so image bumps do not trigger app builds.

exercises.prompt: Show whether the Argo CD app matches Git.

questions.question: In pull-based GitOps, who applies manifests?
questions.explain: The in-cluster controller pulls from Git, so CI needs no cluster credentials.

questions.question: What does selfHeal do?
options: Reverts manual changes that drift from Git
questions.explain: selfHeal reapplies Git state when live objects are edited.

questions.question: What does prune do?
questions.explain: Pruning deletes cluster objects no longer present in the source.

questions.question: Best way to roll back in GitOps?
questions.explain: The Git history is the source of truth; revert the commit and let it reconcile.

lessons.title: Progressive delivery: rolling, blue/green and canary
lessons.summary: Compare release strategies and implement canary and blue/green with Argo Rollouts and Gateway API traffic splitting.
objectives: Compare rolling, blue/green and canary on risk and cost
Write an Argo Rollout with analysis-gated steps
Split traffic by weight with a Gateway API HTTPRoute

sections.title: Choosing how much risk to take
sections.body:
A **rolling update** replaces pods gradually and is built into Deployments, but traffic shifts in proportion to pod counts and rollback means another rollout. **Blue/green** runs the new version beside the old and flips a Service or route at once, giving instant rollback at double the capacity. A **canary** sends a small, measured share of traffic to the new version and promotes only if metrics stay healthy.

Progressive delivery adds automation to canaries: weights, pauses and metric checks decide whether to continue or abort.

sections.title: Strategy comparison
head: Strategy
Traffic shift
Rollback
Extra cost
Needs
rows: All at once at the switch
Copy of traffic, no responses used

sections.title: About this example: an Argo Rollout
sections.body: This is a complete Argo Rollouts `Rollout` (the Argo Rollouts controller and CRD must be installed), a drop-in replacement for a Deployment. It runs a canary with weights and pauses, and uses an analysis between steps. Look at `strategy.canary.steps`, at `trafficRouting` which hands weight control to the Gateway API plugin, and at `stableService`/`canaryService` that identify the two sets of pods.

sections.title: Rollout with canary steps
sections.code:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: shop-api
  namespace: shop-prod
spec:
  replicas: 6
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: shop-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: shop-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/shop/api:1.9.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
  strategy:
    canary:
      stableService: shop-api-stable
      canaryService: shop-api-canary
      trafficRouting:
        plugins:
          argoproj-labs/gatewayAPI:
            httpRoute: shop-api
            namespace: shop-prod
      steps:
        - setWeight: 5
        - pause: {duration: 5m}
        - analysis:
            templates:
              - templateName: success-rate
        - setWeight: 25
        - pause: {duration: 10m}
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: {duration: 10m}

sections.title: About this example: Gateway API weighted routing
sections.body: This complete `HTTPRoute` splits traffic between the stable and canary Services by weight, using only standard Gateway API fields (`gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1`). Rollouts edits the two `weight` values as it moves through the steps. Look at `parentRefs` (which Gateway), the two `backendRefs`, and that weights are relative, so 95 and 5 equal 95% and 5%.

sections.title: HTTPRoute with 95/5 split
sections.code:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: shop-api
  namespace: shop-prod
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: public-gateway
      namespace: gateway-system
  hostnames:
    - shop.example.com
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /api}
      backendRefs:
        - name: shop-api-stable
          port: 80
          weight: 95
        - name: shop-api-canary
          port: 80
          weight: 5

sections.title: About this example: driving a rollout
sections.body: These commands use the `kubectl argo rollouts` plugin to watch, promote and abort. The tree output shows the stable ReplicaSet, the canary ReplicaSet and the current step. Look at `Status: Paused` and `SetWeight`, which tell you which step is waiting, and use `promote` to skip a pause or `abort` to send traffic back to stable.

sections.title: Watch, promote and abort a rollout
sections.code:
kubectl argo rollouts get rollout shop-api -n shop-prod
kubectl argo rollouts promote shop-api -n shop-prod
kubectl argo rollouts abort shop-api -n shop-prod

sections.title: Pick what your platform supports
sections.body: Argo Rollouts also supports NGINX, Istio, SMI and ALB traffic routing, and blue/green via `strategy.blueGreen`. Flagger is the Flux-aligned equivalent. Without any controller, you can approximate a canary with two Deployments behind one Service, but the split follows pod counts, not percentages. Database migrations must be backward compatible, because old and new versions run together.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of blue/green?
questions.explain: The old version stays running, so you switch back immediately.

questions.question: What does a failed AnalysisRun do?
options: Aborts the rollout and returns to stable
questions.explain: Failed analysis aborts and reverts traffic to the stable ReplicaSet.

questions.question: Why can't a plain Deployment do an exact 5% canary?
questions.explain: kube-proxy balances across ready endpoints, so share depends on replica ratio.

questions.question: In HTTPRoute, backendRef weights are...
questions.explain: Weights are relative; the share is weight divided by the sum.

lessons.title: CI pipelines for Kubernetes and promotion
lessons.summary: Build, scan, render and validate manifests in CI, then promote one immutable artifact across environments.
objectives: Design a pipeline that builds, scans, renders and validates
Use kubeconform, kubectl diff and server-side dry-run

sections.title: What a delivery pipeline must prove
sections.body:
A Kubernetes pipeline answers four questions before anything reaches production: does the image build and is it free of known critical vulnerabilities, do the rendered manifests match the API schemas, will the live API server accept them, and what exactly will change. Each question maps to a cheap automated check, ordered from fastest to slowest.

The key principle is **build once, promote many**: one image identified by digest moves through staging and production; only configuration differs.

sections.title: Pipeline stages
head: Stage
Tool and command
Catches
Needs cluster?

sections.title: About this example: a CI workflow
sections.body: This is a GitHub Actions workflow file (not a Kubernetes manifest, so shown as text) with build, scan and validate jobs. Look at the image being tagged with the commit SHA and its digest captured as an output, at `--exit-code 1` making Trivy fail the build, and at kubeconform validating rendered YAML with `-strict` against Kubernetes 1.31 schemas plus the datree CRD catalog.

sections.title: .github/workflows/delivery.yaml
sections.code:
name: delivery
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    outputs:
      digest: ${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with: {registry: registry.example.com, username: ci, password: '${{ secrets.REGISTRY_TOKEN }}'}
      - id: push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          push: true
          tags: registry.example.com/shop/api:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Scan
        run: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 registry.example.com/shop/api@${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: kubectl kustomize overlays/staging > /tmp/staging.yaml
      - run: kubeconform -strict -summary -kubernetes-version 1.31.0 -schema-location default -schema-location 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datreeio/CRDs-catalog/main/{{.Group}}/{{.ResourceKind}}_{{.ResourceAPIVersion}}.json' /tmp/staging.yaml

sections.title: About this example: validation output
sections.body: These commands run the checks locally the same way CI does. `kubeconform` is purely offline; `--dry-run=server` sends the object through the real API server, running admission webhooks and quota checks but persisting nothing; `kubectl diff` shows the change. In the output, look at the kubeconform summary counts and at the per-object `server dry run` lines.

sections.title: kubeconform, server dry-run and diff
sections.code:
kubectl kustomize overlays/prod | kubeconform -strict -summary -kubernetes-version 1.31.0 -
kubectl kustomize overlays/prod | kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f -

sections.title: About this example: promotion by pull request
sections.body: This is the deploy repository layout and the single edit that promotes a release. Promotion changes the image tag or digest in the next environment's overlay, via an automated pull request, so reviews and GitOps handle the rest. Look at the `images` entry that pins a digest rather than a mutable tag; every environment then runs byte-identical content.

sections.title: Promoting staging to prod
sections.code:
# overlays/staging/kustomization.yaml (updated by CI after build)
images:
  - name: registry.example.com/shop/api
    digest: sha256:3b1f0e8c9d52a7f4c8b6e1d0a9f27c43e5b8d6a1c0f9e2b7d4a3c8e1f6b50a92

# promotion job: copy the same digest to prod and open a PR
cd overlays/prod
kustomize edit set image registry.example.com/shop/api@sha256:3b1f0e8c9d52a7f4c8b6e1d0a9f27c43e5b8d6a1c0f9e2b7d4a3c8e1f6b50a92
gh pr create --title 'Promote shop-api to prod' --body 'Digest verified in staging'

sections.title: Never deploy from a mutable tag or unscanned image
sections.body: `latest` and re-pushed tags make rollbacks and audits meaningless. Pin by digest, sign images (cosign) and verify them with an admission policy (Kyverno or ValidatingAdmissionPolicy). Also give CI the least access it needs: a pull-based GitOps flow needs none to the cluster, while push-based flows should use short-lived OIDC credentials.

exercises.title: Server dry run
exercises.prompt: Check what the API server would do with the overlay.
exercises.hint: server mode runs admission; client does not.

questions.question: What does --dry-run=server check that kubeconform cannot?
options: Admission, quota and immutable field rules
questions.explain: The real API server runs admission and validation with current cluster state.

questions.question: Why promote by digest?
options: Immutable, identical artifact in every environment
questions.explain: Digests cannot be re-pointed like tags.

questions.question: What exit behaviour does kubectl diff have when changes exist?
questions.explain: Exit code 1 means differences were found; above 1 means an error.

questions.question: Which stage needs no cluster access?
questions.explain: kubeconform validates rendered YAML against schemas offline.
